title: Data Science Core Skills
text:
What is here
Welcome. This is a self-study course in the mathematics, statistics and Python you will need for an MSc in Data Science. It is open, free, and designed to be worked through before your course begins.
You do not need to have done any of it to start your degree. It exists because students arrive from very different backgrounds — some have not seen calculus in a decade, some have never written a line of code, some have both and want to refresh — and because arriving with these ideas already familiar makes the first term substantially easier.
Thirty-five short units across three tracks.
Python comes first, and that is deliberate. Every mathematics and statistics unit ends by checking its own claim in a few lines of code — a derivative against a numerical estimate, a confidence interval against a simulation. Those checks are the most useful part of each unit, and they are only useful if you can read them.
Every unit is built to the same shape and sized for one sitting: a few pages to read, a worked example, exercises with full solutions, a short piece of code that checks the idea, and five questions to test yourself. Nothing is hidden in an appendix, because there are no appendices.

How much time it takes
Working through everything takes roughly 65 to 70 hours. How you spread that is up to you, and the units do not expire:

Four weeks, most of a working week — the intensive route, if you have the summer free.
Ten weeks, an evening or two a week — the steady route, and the one most people take.
Only what the diagnostic flags — perfectly legitimate. If you last used matrices two years ago, refresh matrices and leave the rest.

title: Data Science Core Skills
text:
About the data
Every worked example uses one small table describing a fictional previous cohort: their prior background, hours of practice, and final scores. The data are invented. They describe no real student and no real cohort, and the script that generates them is included in the repository so you can see exactly how they were made.
Using one dataset throughout means you never have to learn a new context to follow an example — by the third unit you will know what the columns mean, and you can spend your attention on the idea instead.

title: How to use this
section: How to work through a unit
text:
How to work through a unit
Read it once without stopping, then go back and do the exercises. The reading takes twenty minutes or so; the exercises take longer, and they are where the learning actually happens.
Three habits are worth building deliberately:
Predict before you run. When you reach a piece of code, decide what it will print before you run it. When you get it wrong you have learned something specific; when you get it right you have earned some confidence.
Reveal solutions late. The solutions are one click away, which makes them very easy to look at too early. Write something down first — even something you suspect is wrong. Comparing a wrong attempt with a correct solution teaches far more than reading a correct solution cold.
Say the answer in words. If you can compute a derivative but cannot say what it means, you are not finished. Every worked example in these notes ends with an interpretation for exactly this reason.

title: How to use this
text:
What you can skip
Quite a lot, possibly. The diagnostic exists to tell you what.
The three tracks are largely independent, and within each one the units say what they assume. If a unit’s Before you start list holds no surprises and you can do its quick check, you can move on. Nobody is marking this, and there is no credit for reading pages you did not need.
The tracks are presented in the order Python, Mathematics, Statistics. That is a suggestion, not a rule, but it is the order the material was built for: the mathematics and statistics units check themselves in code, so a little Python first makes everything after it more useful. If you already program, skim the Python track for the NumPy and pandas units and move on.
Three dependencies cross between tracks, and the units flag them:

Every Mathematics and Statistics unit has a Check it in Python block, which assumes roughly Python 1–5.
Statistics 5 (random variables) uses integration from Mathematics 7.
Statistics 11 (regression) uses least squares from Mathematics 11.

title: How to use this
text:
If you get stuck
Getting stuck is not a signal that you are behind. It is the ordinary texture of learning mathematics, and everybody doing this course is experiencing it.
Try, in this order: reread the Before you start list and follow the link back; work the numbers on paper rather than in your head; try the exercise with smaller or simpler numbers first; leave it and come back tomorrow, which works far more often than it has any right to.
If it still will not come, note it down and move on. Several ideas here only land in retrospect, once you have seen what they are used for.

title: How to use this
text:
A note on honesty
There is no assessment attached to any of this, which means there is nothing to be gained by getting through it quickly. You can have an AI assistant produce every answer on this site in a few minutes and learn nothing at all.
If you use one — and it is a reasonable tool — use it the way you would use a tutor rather than an answer key: ask it to explain a step you did not follow, ask it why your attempt was wrong, ask it for another example of the same type. Then close it and do the next exercise yourself.

title: Set up Python
text:
1. Install Python
You can read the mathematics without running anything. But every unit ends with a short piece of code that checks the idea, and typing those in yourself — and breaking them, and fixing them — is worth a great deal.
This takes about an hour, once. At the end you will have one folder on your computer that holds everything for this course, and a program called JupyterLab open in your web browser, where you will write and run all of your code.
Install Python 3.12 — not the newest version. The large yellow button on python.org offers a newer Python, and the packages in step 4 will refuse to install on it. Use one of these instead:
Python 3.11 works equally well. Anything older or newer does not.
Open the file you downloaded and follow the installer. On Windows, tick “Add python.exe to PATH” on the first screen — it lets the terminal find Python. It is easy to miss and awkward to fix afterwards.

title: Set up Python
text:
Windows: Python 3.12.10 for Windows
macOS: Python 3.12.10 for macOS
Linux: run python3 --version first; if it says 3.11 or 3.12, you have what you need.

title: Set up Python
text:
2. Open a terminal
A terminal is a window where you type instructions instead of clicking.

Windows: press the Start button, type powershell, and open Windows PowerShell.
macOS: press ⌘ + Space, type terminal, and press Return.

A window opens with a line of text ending in a blinking cursor. That line is the prompt: it is waiting for you. Type a command, press Enter (Return on a Mac), and it runs. Nothing you type here will break your computer.
A terminal is always inside one folder, and it starts in your home folder — the one with your user name. Every command you run happens there unless you move.

title: Set up Python
text:
3. Make your course folder
Type these one at a time, pressing Enter after each:
mkdir bootcamp
cd bootcamp
mkdir makes a folder called bootcamp inside your home folder. cd moves the terminal into it. You can see it in the ordinary way too: in File Explorer, open your user folder; in Finder, choose Go ▸ Home. It is empty for now.
Now make an environment — a private copy of Python for this course, so that nothing you install here can disturb anything else on your machine:
python -m venv .venv
On macOS and Linux, type python3 instead of python on this one line.
Then switch the environment on (“activate” it):
# Windows PowerShell
.venv\Scripts\activate

# macOS or Linux
source .venv/bin/activate
Your prompt now starts with (.venv). From here on, plain python works on every system.
If Windows answers “running scripts is disabled on this system”, type this, press Enter, answer Y, and then activate again:
Set-ExecutionPolicy -Scope CurrentUser RemoteSigned

title: Set up Python
text:
4. Install the packages
Python on its own does arithmetic and text. Packages are extra, free libraries that other people have written — for tables of data, for charts, for statistics. Install the five this course uses:
python -m pip install numpy==1.26.4 pandas==2.3.3 matplotlib==3.10.8 scipy==1.17.0 jupyterlab==4.5.3
This downloads quite a lot and takes a few minutes. The == numbers ask for exact versions, so that the numbers you get match the numbers printed in these notes.

title: Set up Python
text:
5. Start JupyterLab
jupyter lab
Your web browser opens a new tab. That is JupyterLab. It is running on your own computer, not on the internet, and the panel on the left is your bootcamp folder.
Leave the terminal window open — closing it stops JupyterLab.

title: Set up Python
text:
6. Get the data
Every example in these notes uses one small table.

In JupyterLab, click the New Folder button above the file panel and name the folder data. Double-click it to go inside.
Download cohort.csv and background_meta.csv. Your browser saves them to your Downloads folder.
Back in JupyterLab, still inside data, click the Upload button (the upward arrow above the file panel) and choose both files from Downloads.

Click the folder icon at the start of the path above the file panel to return to bootcamp.

title: Set up Python
text:
7. Check it all works
In JupyterLab’s Launcher tab, click Python 3 (ipykernel) under Notebook. A notebook opens with one empty box, called a cell. Click in it, paste this, and press Shift + Enter to run it:
import sys, numpy, pandas
print(sys.version.split()[0], numpy.__version__, pandas.__version__)
print(pandas.read_csv("data/cohort.csv").shape)
You should see:
3.12.10 1.26.4 2.3.3
(240, 7)
The first number may differ if you installed a different 3.12 or 3.11. If you see those two lines, you are set up, and everything else in this course happens in JupyterLab.

title: Set up Python
text:
Every time you come back
JupyterLab needs starting again after you restart your computer or close the terminal. Open a terminal and type the same three lines each time:
# Windows PowerShell
cd bootcamp
.venv\Scripts\activate
jupyter lab

# macOS or Linux
cd bootcamp
source .venv/bin/activate
jupyter lab
Save your notebooks inside bootcamp, and code in these notes that reads data/cohort.csv will find the file.

title: Set up Python
text:
When something goes wrong
It very often does, and the error message is usually more helpful than it looks.
Read the last line first. A Python error prints a long report called a traceback, but the final line names the problem.
ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'pandas' means Python cannot see the packages from step 4 — almost always because the environment was not active. In the terminal, check the prompt shows (.venv). If you were in JupyterLab, close it, activate, and start it again.
FileNotFoundError for data/cohort.csv means your notebook is not in the bootcamp folder, or the files are not inside data. Look at the file panel: you should see data next to your notebook, and the two files inside it.
No such file or directory when activating means the terminal is not in bootcamp. Type cd bootcamp first.
Step 4 fails with a long error — often ending in metadata-generation-failed, Unknown compiler, or No matching distribution found — almost always means the wrong Python. Check with python --version. If it is not 3.11 or 3.12, install 3.12 from the links in step 1, delete the .venv folder inside bootcamp, and repeat from python -m venv .venv in step 3 — without the mkdir, since the folder already exists.
python: command not found on macOS or Linux means you need python3 for the one line that creates the environment. On Windows it usually means the PATH box was missed during installation; running the installer again and ticking it is faster than fixing it by hand.
Keep the whole error. If you need to ask someone, the exact text of the last line is the single most useful thing you can give them.
None of this is a test, and struggling with an install says nothing whatsoever about whether you can program. It is the least interesting part of the course and the only part where the computer, not the idea, is the obstacle.

title: The diagnostic
text:
Python
Fifteen questions, about twenty minutes. Its only purpose is to tell you which units you can skip.
It is not a test, nothing is recorded, and there is no pass mark. Answer honestly — the cost of pretending you can do something is that you skip a unit you needed.
How to take it. Work on paper, without a calculator except where one is obviously needed, and without running any code. Write your answer down before opening the solution: an answer you nearly had is not the same as one you had, and only you can tell the difference. Keep a note of which questions you missed; the routing table at the end turns that list into a reading plan.

title: The diagnostic
text:
1. What does this print?
print(3 / 2, 3 // 2, 7 % 3)








TipShow the answer





1.5 1 1
/ always gives a float, // divides and throws away the remainder, and % gives the remainder. If the first one surprised you, that is Python 3 behaving differently from most people’s expectations and from Python 2.
Covers P2.





2. What does this print?
marks = [41, 58, 67, 72, 90]
print(marks[1:3], marks[-1])








TipShow the answer





[58, 67] 90
A slice a:b starts at a and stops before b, so it has \(b - a\) elements. Negative indices count back from the end.
Covers P3.





3. What array does this produce, and what shape is it?
import numpy as np
grid = np.arange(6).reshape(2, 3)
print(grid + np.array([10, 20, 30]))








TipShow the answer





[[10 21 32]
 [13 24 35]]
Shape \((2, 3)\). The one-dimensional array of length 3 is broadcast down both rows. If you expected an error, or expected the addition to go the other way, read the NumPy units.
Covers P6 and P7.





4. A pandas DataFrame df has a column score containing some missing values. What does df[df["score"] > 70]["score"].mean() compute, and what happens to the missing values?








TipShow the answer





It keeps the rows whose score exceeds 70 and averages that column. Rows with a missing score are silently dropped by the comparison — NaN > 70 is False — and .mean() would skip any that survived anyway.
The important half of the answer is “silently”. Nothing warns you, and the count you would have reported is smaller than you think.
Covers P8 and P9.

title: The diagnostic
text:
Mathematics


5. Evaluate \(\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{4} (2i - 1)\).








TipShow the answer





\(1 + 3 + 5 + 7 = 16\).
The notation says “put \(i = 1, 2, 3, 4\) into \(2i - 1\) in turn, and add the results”. If reading it aloud was the hard part rather than the arithmetic, M1 is written for you.
Covers M1.





6. Solve \(2^x = 32\). Then write \(\ln(e^3)\) and \(\log(ab)\) more simply.








TipShow the answer





\(x = 5\), since \(2^5 = 32\). \(\ln(e^3) = 3\), because a logarithm undoes the exponential. \(\log(ab) = \log a + \log b\) — logs turn multiplication into addition, which is the whole reason they exist.
Covers M2.





7. A straight line passes through \((2, 5)\) and \((6, 17)\). What is its gradient, and what does a gradient of 3 mean in words?








TipShow the answer





\((17 - 5)/(6 - 2) = 12/4 = 3\).
In words: for every 1 the input increases, the output increases by 3. If the arithmetic was fine but the sentence was not, do not skip M3 — the sentence is the part everything later depends on.
Covers M3.





8. Differentiate \(f(x) = x^3 - 4x + 1\).








TipShow the answer





\(f'(x) = 3x^2 - 4\).
Bring the power down and reduce it by one; the derivative of a constant is zero.
Covers M4.





9. Where does \(g(x) = x^2 - 6x + 5\) take its smallest value, and what is that value?








TipShow the answer





\(g'(x) = 2x - 6\), which is zero at \(x = 3\). There \(g(3) = 9 - 18 + 5 = -4\).
It is a minimum rather than a maximum because the parabola opens upwards — a check worth making rather than assuming.
Covers M5.





10. Evaluate \(\displaystyle\int_0^2 3x^2\,dx\).








TipShow the answer





\(\bigl[x^3\bigr]_0^2 = 8 - 0 = 8\).
If you also said “that is the area under the curve \(y = 3x^2\) between 0 and 2”, you have the reading that S5 needs.
Covers M7.





11. \(A\) is \(3 \times 4\) and \(B\) is \(4 \times 2\). What is the shape of \(AB\)? What about \(BA\)?








TipShow the answer





\(AB\) is \(3 \times 2\): the inner dimensions (4 and 4) must match and they cancel, leaving the outer ones. \(BA\) does not exist — \(B\) has 2 columns and \(A\) has 3 rows, and \(2 \ne 3\).
Shape arithmetic is most of what goes wrong in practice, and it is checkable before you run anything.
Covers M8 and M9.





12. Solve \(2x + y = 7\) and \(x - y = 2\).








TipShow the answer





Add the two equations: \(3x = 9\), so \(x = 3\), and then \(y = 1\).
Check both: \(2(3) + 1 = 7\) ✓ and \(3 - 1 = 2\) ✓. Substituting your answer back is a five-second habit that catches most arithmetic slips.
Covers M10.

title: The diagnostic
text:
Statistics


13. For the values \(4, 4, 5, 9, 13\): give the mean, the median, and say which of the two is larger and why.








TipShow the answer





Mean \(= 35/5 = 7\). Median \(= 5\) (the middle value once sorted).
The mean is larger because the two big values pull it up, while the median notices only that they are above the middle. (For completeness, the sample standard deviation is 3.94, dividing by \(n - 1 = 4\).)
Covers S2.





14. Of 200 students, 80 use the library weekly and 60 of those 80 passed. Of the 120 who do not, 60 passed. What is the probability that a student passed given that they use the library? And that they use the library given that they passed?








TipShow the answer





\(P(\text{pass} \mid \text{library}) = 60/80 = 0.75\).
For the other one, count all the passers: \(60 + 60 = 120\). So \(P(\text{library} \mid \text{pass}) = 60/120 = 0.50\).
Two different numbers from the same 60 students, because the denominator changed. If those came out equal, S4 is the most valuable unit on this site for you.
Covers S4.





15. A sample of 64 measurements has a standard deviation of 16.

What is the standard error of the mean?
The resulting 95% confidence interval is \((10.2, 13.8)\). Is it correct to say “there is a 95% probability the population mean lies between 10.2 and 13.8”?









TipShow the answer






\(16/\sqrt{64} = 16/8 = 2\).
No. The 95% describes the procedure: across many repeated studies, 95% of the intervals built this way contain the true mean. This particular interval either contains it or does not.

If (a) was fine and (b) was not, read S8 — the distinction it draws is the one most often got wrong in published work.
Covers S7 and S8.

Three things the table cannot tell you.
A confident wrong answer is worse than a blank. If you were sure and wrong, read the unit rather than skimming it: what needs replacing is a belief, not a gap.
S1 and S12 are not on the table, because no short question tests them. They are about choosing what to ask and recognising how an answer goes wrong, and they are the two units most likely to change how you work. Read both regardless of how you scored.
Seven more units have no question of their own: P5, P10, P11, M12, S6, S10 and S11. Read each one unless you can do its Before you start quick check without looking.
If you missed most of a track’s questions, ignore the table for that track and read it in order from its first unit. The table is for skipping what you know, not for choosing a path through what you do not.
Nobody skips everything. If you answered all fifteen comfortably, you do not need the mechanics — but the Common wrong turns block in each unit is worth twenty minutes on its own, and it is where most of the material that is new to experienced readers lives.

title: 1. Getting Python running
text:
1.1 Before you start
Nothing. This is the first unit, and it assumes you have never written a line of code.
It does assume you have worked through Set up Python, which takes about an hour and leaves you with a bootcamp folder and JupyterLab.
Quick check. Can you start JupyterLab and see your data folder in its file panel?

title: 1. Getting Python running
text:
TipShow the answer





Open a terminal and type, pressing Enter after each line:
cd bootcamp
.venv\Scripts\activate          # Windows PowerShell
source .venv/bin/activate       # macOS or Linux, instead of the line above
jupyter lab
A browser tab opens, and the panel on the left lists data. If any line fails, the setup page’s When something goes wrong section covers the usual causes.

title: 1. Getting Python running
text:
1.2 The idea
Python is a language for giving a computer instructions. You write instructions in a plain text file; a program called the interpreter reads that file and carries them out, one line at a time, top to bottom.
That is genuinely all that happens. There is no compilation step to think about and no magic. When something goes wrong, it went wrong on one specific line, and Python will tell you which.
There are two ways to run instructions, and you will use both:

A script is a file ending in .py. You run the whole thing at once. Use scripts when a task should run start-to-finish the same way every time.
A notebook is a file ending in .ipynb, made of cells you run one at a time, with output appearing underneath. Use notebooks to explore, and to mix explanation with code.

These notes are written as notebooks-in-spirit: every code block you see was actually run, and its output is printed underneath.

title: 1. Getting Python running
text:
1.3 The mechanics

1. What setup gave you
Three things, each of which you will lean on in every unit:

Python itself — the interpreter.
An environment, the .venv folder inside bootcamp. venv stands for virtual environment: a private copy of Python with this course’s packages in it. You must activate it each time you open a new terminal. Forgetting is the single commonest cause of “but I installed that already”.
JupyterLab, which runs in your browser and is where you write both scripts and notebooks.

Do not repeat the setup commands here. Typing mkdir bootcamp again from inside bootcamp makes a second bootcamp inside the first, and code that looks for data/cohort.csv stops finding it.


2. Your first program, as a script
In JupyterLab, choose File ▸ New ▸ Python File. An empty editor opens. Type one line:
print("Hello from my own machine")
Choose File ▸ Save Python File As…, name it hello.py, and save. It appears in the file panel, inside bootcamp.
To run it, choose File ▸ New ▸ Terminal. This terminal opens already inside bootcamp and uses the same Python as JupyterLab. Type:
python hello.py
and press Enter. The line of text appears underneath.


3. The same line, in a notebook
Choose File ▸ New ▸ Notebook (pick Python 3 (ipykernel) if asked). Type the same print(...) line into the empty cell and press Shift + Enter. The output appears directly under the cell, and a new empty cell opens below it.
That is the whole difference: a script runs top to bottom in one go; a notebook runs whichever cell you choose, when you choose. Every code block in these notes can be pasted into a notebook cell.


4. Read the traceback
Now make it fail on purpose. Change hello.py to this, save it, and run it again:
temperature = "22C"
print(temperature + 5)
Python stops and prints a traceback. It looks alarming and is not. It is a report with a fixed shape, and you read it from the bottom.

temperature = "22C"
print(temperature + 5)


---------------------------------------------------------------------------
TypeError                                 Traceback (most recent call last)
Cell In[1], line 2
      1 temperature = "22C"
----> 2 print(temperature + 5)

TypeError: can only concatenate str (not "int") to str











Figure 5.1: Every traceback has this shape. The last line names what went wrong; the lines above say where. Read the bottom line first, then look at the line of your own code it points to.





The bottom line is the answer: you tried to join a piece of text to a number, and Python will not guess what you meant. The lines above tell you it happened in hello.py, on line 2.

title: 1. Getting Python running
text:
1.4 Worked example
A traceback, diagnosed and fixed.
Suppose you are asked to add up three measurements and one of them came from a text file, so it is still text:

measurements = [12.5, 13.1, "12.9"]
total = sum(measurements)


---------------------------------------------------------------------------
TypeError                                 Traceback (most recent call last)
Cell In[3], line 2
      1 measurements = [12.5, 13.1, "12.9"]
----> 2 total = sum(measurements)

TypeError: unsupported operand type(s) for +: 'float' and 'str'



Work through it in the fixed order.
Bottom line first. TypeError: unsupported operand type(s) for +: 'float' and 'str'. Something tried to add a number to a piece of text.
Which line? The traceback points at the sum(...) call.
What actually reached it? Look at the data:

measurements = [12.5, 13.1, "12.9"]
for value in measurements:
    print(repr(value), type(value).__name__)

12.5 float
13.1 float
'12.9' str


There it is. The third value is '12.9' with quotation marks — text that looks like a number. repr() shows the quotation marks that print() hides, which is why it is the right tool for this question.
The fix, stated deliberately rather than patched:

measurements = [12.5, 13.1, "12.9"]
numbers = [float(value) for value in measurements]
print(sum(numbers))

38.5


Notice what we did not do: we did not delete the awkward value, and we did not wrap the whole thing in something that swallows the error. We found out what was actually in the data and converted it on purpose. That habit is worth more than any syntax in this unit.

title: 1. Getting Python running
text:
1.5 Try it yourself

Exercise 1 Predict the final line of the traceback, then run it.
print(x)






TipShow the solution





NameError: name 'x' is not defined.
Python has no idea what x is, because nothing has ever assigned a value to that name. This is different from a TypeError, which means the name does exist but holds something the operation cannot use.





Exercise 2 This one fails before it runs at all. Why is that different?
print("Hello






TipShow the solution





SyntaxError: unterminated string literal.
The closing quotation mark is missing, so Python cannot even parse the file into instructions. A SyntaxError is raised before anything executes, which is why you can get one from a line far below code that would otherwise have run.
The practical tell: if nothing at all printed, suspect a syntax error. If some output appeared and then it stopped, the program was running and hit a problem partway.





Exercise 3 You run a script and get ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'pandas', but you installed pandas ten minutes ago. What is the most likely cause?






TipShow the solution





You are not in the environment you installed into. Check whether your prompt still shows (.venv); if not, activate it again. If this happened in JupyterLab, it was started from a terminal where the environment was not active: close it, activate, and start it again.
The general shape of this error: Python is looking, and not finding, so either it was never installed or you are asking a different Python. Confirm which interpreter is running with the check in the next section.

title: 1. Getting Python running
text:
1.6 Check it in Python
Every other unit ends by checking a claim. This one checks your setup, which is the claim that matters here.

import sys
import numpy, pandas, matplotlib, scipy

print("python     ", sys.version.split()[0])
print("interpreter", sys.executable)
for package in (numpy, pandas, matplotlib, scipy):
    print(f"{package.__name__:<11}", package.__version__)

python      3.11.14
interpreter /home/hyperspace/anaconda3/bin/python
numpy       1.26.4
pandas      2.3.3
matplotlib  3.10.8
scipy       1.17.0


Two things to look at. The version should start with 3.12 or 3.11 — these notes were run on 3.11, which is why the output above says so. And the interpreter path should point inside your .venv folder — if it points somewhere else, you are running the wrong Python, and that explains almost every “but I installed it” problem you will hit.
Keep this snippet. When you ask anyone for help, the answer is more useful if you paste its output with your question.

title: 1. Getting Python running
text:
1.7 Common wrong turns

Where this usually goes wrong

Reading the traceback from the top

The top is the least useful part. The bottom line names the problem; work upwards only if you need to know how execution got there.

Assuming an error means you cannot program

Everyone who writes code sees errors constantly, including people who have done it for thirty years. An error is the program telling you something specific and true. It is information, not a verdict.

Installing the newest Python

The obvious download button gives a version newer than the pinned packages support, and pip install then fails, usually with a long build error that never mentions the Python version. Check python --version, install 3.12, delete .venv, and recreate it.

Forgetting to activate the environment

If your prompt does not begin (.venv), you are using a different Python with different packages. This causes more confusion in week one than any other single thing.

Typing the prompt character

Examples sometimes show $ or > at the start of a line. That is the prompt, not part of the command. Type only what follows it.

Changing several things at once when stuck

Then you cannot tell which change helped. Make one change, run it, look at the result.

Pasting a fix you do not understand

It may work today and leave you unable to fix it tomorrow. Before you keep any snippet — from a forum, or from an assistant — make sure you can say what each line does.

the first b. the last c. the one naming your file d. all of them, in order

(b) the last. It names the exception type and the message — what actually went wrong. The lines above tell you where, which only matters once you know what.
A SyntaxError means Python could not read your file as instructions, so nothing ran at all. A NameError means the file ran fine until it reached a name that had never been given a value.
It keeps this project’s packages separate from everything else on your machine, so installing something here cannot break something there.
Whether the environment is active — does your prompt show (.venv)? Then confirm with sys.executable that the running interpreter is the one inside it.
No. A syntax error is raised before any code executes, so no output would have appeared. Output followed by a stop means the program was running and hit a problem partway through — which is a useful diagnostic in itself.





Where this shows up next

run a script or a notebook cell — P1;
read the last line of a traceback — P1.


print(3 + 4)
print("3" + "4")






TipShow the answer





7, then 34.
The + symbol does two different jobs depending on what sits either side of it: arithmetic on numbers, joining on text. That is not Python being inconsistent — it is the type deciding the meaning, which is exactly this unit’s subject.
crumbs: 6  2. Values, names and types

title: 2. Values, names and types
text:
2.2 The idea
Writing x = 5 does not put 5 into a box called x. It creates the value 5 and attaches the name x to it, like a luggage label. The name is not the thing.
That distinction sounds academic until you meet its consequences, so it is worth a picture:








Figure 6.1: Assignment attaches a name to a value. Two names can label the same value; reassigning one moves that label without touching the value or the other name.





In code:

count = 5
total = count      # a second label on the same value
count = 9          # move the first label to a different value

print("count:", count)
print("total:", total)

count: 9
total: 5


total still refers to 5. Reassigning count moved one label; it did not reach inside total and change anything. For the simple values in this unit that is easy to accept, and in P3 it becomes something you must think about.
crumbs: 6  2. Values, names and types

title: 2. Values, names and types
text:
2.3 The mechanics

The five types to recognise

values = [42, 3.14, True, "hello", None]
for value in values:
    print(f"{repr(value):<8} {type(value).__name__}")

42       int
3.14     float
True     bool
'hello'  str
None     NoneType



int — a whole number, of any size. Python will happily hold a 200-digit integer.
float — a number with a decimal part, stored to finite precision. More on that below, because it will bite you.
bool — True or False. Use these for logical state, not as 1 and 0.
str — text, in quotation marks. "5" is text; 5 is a number.
None — the deliberate absence of a value. Not zero, not an empty string; a positive statement that there is nothing here.



Converting on purpose

reading = "22.5"
print(float(reading) + 5)

27.5


Conversion works when the value has a sensible reading in the target type, and raises when it does not:

float("22C")


---------------------------------------------------------------------------
ValueError                                Traceback (most recent call last)
Cell In[5], line 1
----> 1 float("22C")

ValueError: could not convert string to float: '22C'



That failure is a feature. Python could have guessed 22 and thrown away the C, and then your temperature data would silently lose its units.


Floats are approximate
This is the one that surprises everyone:

print(0.1 + 0.2)
print(0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3)

0.30000000000000004
False


Nothing is broken. Computers store numbers in binary, and 0.1 has no exact binary representation — just as 1/3 has no exact decimal one. The tiny error is real and unavoidable.
The consequence for you is a rule: never test computed floats with ==. Test whether they are close enough:

import numpy as np
print(np.isclose(0.1 + 0.2, 0.3))

True


Integers are exact, so == is fine for them. It is floats that need care, and this is why M4 checks a derivative with np.isclose rather than ==.


f-strings
To build text that contains values, put an f before the quotation mark and the values in braces:

name = "Life sciences"
mean = 60.5137
count = 57

print(f"{name}: mean {mean:.2f} over {count} students")

Life sciences: mean 60.51 over 57 students


:.2f means “as a float, to two decimal places”. This is how every number in these notes is printed, and it saves you from reporting a mean to twelve digits you cannot justify.


Naming
A name should say what the value is, and what unit it is in:

temperature_c = 21.5
elapsed_seconds = 90
proportion_passed = 0.83

print(f"{temperature_c}°C, {elapsed_seconds}s, {proportion_passed:.0%} passed")

21.5°C, 90s, 83% passed


t = 21.5 is shorter and tells a reader — including you in a fortnight — nothing. Units in the name have prevented more errors than any other habit in this course.

title: 2. Values, names and types
text:
2.4 Worked example
Reading a value whose type is not what you assumed.
The cohort file is text on disk. Every column arrives as characters, and something has to decide what they mean. Watch what happens when that decision is skipped:

score_from_file = "68.4"
bonus = 5

print("what we have:", repr(score_from_file), type(score_from_file).__name__)

what we have: '68.4' str



score_from_file + bonus


---------------------------------------------------------------------------
TypeError                                 Traceback (most recent call last)
Cell In[11], line 1
----> 1 score_from_file + bonus

TypeError: can only concatenate str (not "int") to str



The error is exactly the one from P1. Now convert on purpose, and check:

score = float(score_from_file)
print("converted:", repr(score), type(score).__name__)
print("with bonus:", score + bonus)

converted: 68.4 float
with bonus: 73.4


One thing worth noticing before you move on. "68.4" + "5" would not have raised — it would have produced "68.45", silently, and everything downstream would have been wrong without a single error message.

print(repr(score_from_file + "5"))

'68.45'


An error that stops you is a good outcome. The dangerous case is the operation that succeeds and means something else.

title: 2. Values, names and types
text:
2.5 Try it yourself

Exercise 1 Predict each result, then run them.
print(7 / 2)
print(7 // 2)
print(type(7 / 2).__name__)






TipShow the solution





3.5, 3, float.
/ always produces a float, even when the division is exact — 4 / 2 gives 2.0, not 2. // is floor division: it divides and rounds down to a whole number.
The third line is the one people get wrong. 7 / 2 is a float because / always is.





Exercise 2 Why does the first of these print False and the second True?
print(0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3)
print(1 + 2 == 3)






TipShow the solution





The second uses integers, which are stored exactly, so the comparison is exact.
The first uses floats. 0.1 and 0.2 cannot be represented exactly in binary, so their sum lands a hair away from 0.3 — about 5.6 × 10⁻¹⁷ above it. == asks whether they are identical, and they are not.
Use np.isclose for computed floats. Reserve == for integers, strings, and booleans.





Exercise 3 A colleague stores “no reading was taken” as the number -999. Give two distinct reasons None would be better, and say when -999 might still be forced on you.






TipShow the solution





Two reasons:

-999 participates in arithmetic. Take a mean and it silently drags the answer down; nothing warns you. None cannot be added to anything, so the mistake becomes an error you can see.
-999 is indistinguishable from a genuine measurement of −999. If the quantity could ever legitimately take that value, the two meanings are now merged and cannot be separated.

When it is forced on you: a legacy file format or an instrument that emits a sentinel. Then convert it to a proper missing value as you load the data, record how many you converted, and never let the sentinel reach a calculation. P9 does exactly this.

title: 2. Values, names and types
text:
2.6 Check it in Python
Two habits, both one line each.
Ask what you actually have rather than assuming:

mystery = "12.9"
print(repr(mystery), "→", type(mystery).__name__)

'12.9' → str


repr() rather than print(), because print("12.9") and print(12.9) look identical on screen while repr shows the quotation marks that distinguish them.
Compare computed floats with a tolerance, and see the difference the choice makes:

total = 0.1 + 0.2
print("exact equality :", total == 0.3)
print("np.isclose     :", np.isclose(total, 0.3))
print("the gap        :", total - 0.3)

exact equality : False
np.isclose     : True
the gap        : 5.551115123125783e-17


The gap is about 5.6 × 10⁻¹⁷ — far too small to matter for any measurement, and far too large for == to ignore.
crumbs: 6  2. Values, names and types

title: 2. Values, names and types
text:
2.7 Common wrong turns

Where this usually goes wrong

Testing computed floats with ==

Arithmetic on floats accumulates tiny errors. Use np.isclose, and choose a tolerance that means something for your data.

Assuming a number-looking thing is a number

"5" is text. It arrives that way from files, forms and web pages. Convert deliberately and check the type when a result surprises you.

Treating None as zero or as an empty string

None means nothing was recorded. Zero is a measurement. Conflating them changes your answers and hides the fact that data is missing.

Using a sentinel like -999 for missing data

It survives into every calculation it touches. If a format forces it on you, convert it the moment you load the file.

Naming variables x, df, data, temp

You will not remember what they held. temperature_c costs eleven characters and carries the unit with it.

Assuming print shows you the type

print shows a value’s appearance. "12.9" and 12.9 look the same. Use repr() or type() when the distinction matters.

title: 2. Values, names and types
text:
2.8 Check yourself
Answers are at the foot of the page.



What is the type of 7 / 7?

int b. float c. bool d. depends on the values





a = [1, 2], then b = a. Has b got its own copy of the list, or another label on the same one?




Give a case where "5" + "5" is a bug even though nothing raises.




Why is float("22C") raising an error better than it guessing 22?




Someone reports a mean of -142.7 from scores that should lie between 0 and

What would you check first?










TipShow the answers






(b) float. / always produces a float, so 7 / 7 is 1.0. Only // gives an integer.
Another label on the same list. Nothing was copied. This matters far more for lists than for numbers, because a list can be changed in place — which is P3’s subject.
Any time the two values are numbers that arrived as text. "5" + "5" gives "55", which is not 10 and not an error. Totals that are wildly too large are a classic symptom of adding numbers that were still strings.
Because guessing would silently discard information — the C might mean Celsius, or a grade, or a data-entry slip. An error forces you to decide what the value means, once, on purpose.
Whether a missing-value sentinel like -999 is in the data and got included in the mean. Count how many values are impossible before doing anything else.





Where this shows up next
P3 puts many values in one container, where the name-versus-value distinction from this unit starts to matter a great deal. P6 adds a fixed type to a whole array at once, which is what makes NumPy fast. P9 converts a whole column deliberately, and records what would not convert.

text:

title: 3. Collections
text:
say what type a value has, and convert it deliberately — P2;
explain what a = b does to names — P2.








TipShow the answer





5. Reassigning a moved one label; b still points at the original value. This unit is where that idea stops being a curiosity.

title: 3. Collections
text:
3.2 The idea
The four containers differ along three questions, and that is the whole of it:








Figure 7.1: The four containers, distinguished by three questions. Answer them for your data and the choice is made.






A list is an ordered, changeable sequence. It is the default, and most of the time it is right.
A tuple is an ordered sequence you cannot change. Use it when a group of values belongs together and should stay put.
A dictionary stores values under keys, so you look things up by name rather than by position.
A set holds unique values with no order. Use it to ask have I seen this before?

title: 3. Collections
text:
3.3 The mechanics

Lists

scores = [68.4, 55.1, 72.0, 61.3]

print(scores[0], scores[-1])        # first and last
print(scores[1:3])                  # a slice: from 1, up to but not including 3
print(len(scores))

68.4 61.3
[55.1, 72.0]
4


Python counts from zero, so the first item is at index 0 and the last is at len(scores) - 1. Negative indices count back from the end, which saves you writing scores[len(scores) - 1].
Slicing takes start:stop, and stop is not included. scores[1:3] gives two items, not three. That convention looks odd for a day and then becomes convenient, because scores[:2] and scores[2:] split the list with no overlap and no gap.
Lists change in place:

scores.append(59.8)
scores[0] = 70.0
print(scores)

[70.0, 55.1, 72.0, 61.3, 59.8]




The part that catches people
Because a list can change in place, two names on the same list see each other’s changes:

original = [1, 2, 3]
alias = original          # another label on the SAME list
alias.append(4)

print("original:", original)
print("alias:   ", alias)

original: [1, 2, 3, 4]
alias:    [1, 2, 3, 4]


That is the P2 picture with real consequences. If you want an independent list, ask for one:

original = [1, 2, 3]
independent = original.copy()
independent.append(4)

print("original:   ", original)
print("independent:", independent)

original:    [1, 2, 3]
independent: [1, 2, 3, 4]




Tuples
Parentheses instead of brackets, and no changing afterwards:

point = (52.24, -0.90)      # latitude, longitude
print(point[0])
point[0] = 0

52.24



---------------------------------------------------------------------------
TypeError                                 Traceback (most recent call last)
Cell In[6], line 3
      1 point = (52.24, -0.90)      # latitude, longitude
      2 print(point[0])
----> 3 point[0] = 0

TypeError: 'tuple' object does not support item assignment



The error is the point of a tuple. A coordinate pair, a date, an RGB colour — things whose parts belong together and should not be edited one at a time.


Dictionaries

student = {"id": "S0042", "background": "Life sciences", "score": 68.4}

print(student["background"])
student["completed"] = True          # add a new key
print(list(student.keys()))

Life sciences
['id', 'background', 'score', 'completed']


Look-up is by key, and student["score"] says what it means in a way that row[2] never will. Asking for a key that does not exist raises:

student["age"]


---------------------------------------------------------------------------
KeyError                                  Traceback (most recent call last)
Cell In[8], line 1
----> 1 student["age"]

KeyError: 'age'



Use .get() when absence is expected rather than exceptional:

print(student.get("age", "not recorded"))

not recorded




Sets

backgrounds = ["Computing", "Life sciences", "Computing", "Social sciences"]
unique = set(backgrounds)

print(unique)
print(len(backgrounds), "values,", len(unique), "distinct")

{'Computing', 'Life sciences', 'Social sciences'}
4 values, 3 distinct


Sets are unordered. The printed order is not sorted and must never be relied on — if you want order, ask for it:

print(sorted(unique))

['Computing', 'Life sciences', 'Social sciences']


Membership testing is what sets are really for, and on a large collection it is enormously faster than scanning a list:

print("Computing" in unique)

True

title: 3. Collections
text:
3.4 Worked example
Summarising the cohort with the right container for each job.

import csv
from pathlib import Path

rows = list(csv.DictReader(Path("data/cohort.csv").open()))
print(len(rows), "rows")
print(rows[0])

240 rows
{'student_id': 'S0001', 'background': 'Mathematics or Physics', 'diagnostic_score': '89.1', 'hours_practice': '12.9', 'final_score': '83.6', 'completed': 'True', 'started_on': '2026-09-23'}


csv.DictReader gives one dictionary per row, keyed by column name — so row["final_score"] rather than row[4]. Note that every value is a string: the file is text, and nothing has yet decided what the columns mean.
Now three questions, each answered by a different container.
Which backgrounds appear? Uniqueness matters, order does not — a set:

backgrounds = {row["background"] for row in rows if row["background"]}
for name in sorted(backgrounds):
    print(" ", name)

  Computing
  Engineering
  Life sciences
  Mathematics or Physics
  Social sciences


What is the mean score in each? Look-up by name — a dictionary of lists:

by_background = {}
skipped = 0

for row in rows:
    group, raw = row["background"], row["final_score"]
    if not group or not raw:
        skipped += 1
        continue
    score = float(raw)
    if not 0 <= score <= 100:
        skipped += 1
        continue
    by_background.setdefault(group, []).append(score)

for name in sorted(by_background):
    scores = by_background[name]
    print(f"  {name:<24} n={len(scores):>3}  mean={sum(scores)/len(scores):5.2f}")
print(f"\n  {skipped} rows skipped")

  Computing                n= 69  mean=65.85
  Engineering              n= 36  mean=67.15
  Life sciences            n= 57  mean=60.51
  Mathematics or Physics   n= 36  mean=75.28
  Social sciences          n= 39  mean=60.21

  3 rows skipped


setdefault creates the empty list the first time a group is seen, so you do not have to check whether the key exists on every row.
Notice the three skipped rows are counted, not silently dropped. That number is part of the result; P9 makes it an audit file.
The five highest scores? Order matters — a sorted list:

all_scores = [s for scores in by_background.values() for s in scores]
print(sorted(all_scores, reverse=True)[:5])

[91.6, 88.8, 88.5, 86.6, 85.3]

title: 3. Collections
text:
3.5 Try it yourself

Exercise 1 Predict the output, then run it.
values = [10, 20, 30, 40, 50]
print(values[1:4])
print(values[:2])
print(values[-2:])






TipShow the solution





[20, 30, 40], [10, 20], [40, 50].
The first stops before index 4. The second takes everything up to index 2. The third starts two from the end. Together they show why the convention is convenient: values[:2] + values[2:] reconstructs the whole list exactly.





Exercise 2 This is meant to leave baseline untouched. It does not. Fix it, and say what went wrong.
baseline = [1, 2, 3]
adjusted = baseline
adjusted.append(4)






TipShow the solution





adjusted = baseline makes a second label on the same list, so .append is visible through both names. baseline is now [1, 2, 3, 4].
The fix is to ask for an independent list:
adjusted = baseline.copy()
This is the commonest source of “but I never changed that variable” in a beginner’s code, and it only happens with containers that can change in place — which is why tuples do not have the problem.





Exercise 3 For each, name the container you would use and why in one clause.

Every distinct postcode in a delivery file, to check whether a new one has been seen before.
A student’s id, name and score, passed around as one thing.
Look up a country’s population by its name.
Daily temperature readings, in the order taken.







TipShow the solution






Set — you want uniqueness, and in on a set stays fast however many postcodes there are.
Tuple — the three belong together and should not be edited individually. (A dictionary is also defensible if you want the fields named.)
Dictionary — look-up by key is exactly what it is for.
List — order carries meaning, and you will want to append.

The question to ask each time: do I look things up by position, by name, or just ask whether something is present?

title: 3. Collections
text:
3.6 Check it in Python
Two checks worth building into the way you work.
Confirm you have an independent copy when you meant to:

baseline = [1, 2, 3]
adjusted = baseline.copy()
adjusted.append(4)

assert baseline == [1, 2, 3], "baseline was modified"
print("baseline intact:", baseline)
print("same object?    ", adjusted is baseline)

baseline intact: [1, 2, 3]
same object?     False


is asks whether two names point at the same object; == asks whether two objects have the same contents. Two separate lists holding [1, 2, 3] are == but not is.
Count what you dropped, every time:

raw = ["68.4", "", "72.1", "not recorded", "55.0"]
usable, dropped = [], []
for value in raw:
    try:
        usable.append(float(value))
    except ValueError:
        dropped.append(value)

print(f"kept {len(usable)} of {len(raw)}; dropped {dropped}")
assert len(usable) + len(dropped) == len(raw)

kept 3 of 5; dropped ['', 'not recorded']


The assertion says nothing went missing unaccounted for. It is one line and it turns a silent loss into a loud one.

title: 3. Collections
text:
3.7 Common wrong turns

Where this usually goes wrong

Assuming assignment copies a container

b = a gives a second name for the same list. Use .copy() when you want an independent one, and remember that numbers and strings never have this problem because they cannot be changed in place.

Relying on the order a set prints in

Sets are unordered. The printed order can differ between runs and versions. Call sorted() if you need an order.

Using a list for membership tests on large data

x in some_list scans from the start. x in some_set does not. On a hundred thousand items the difference is dramatic.

Indexing rows by number

row[4] breaks the moment a column is inserted, and it tells a reader nothing. row["final_score"] survives, and explains itself.

Being caught by the exclusive slice end

values[1:3] gives two items. It is a convention worth learning rather than fighting: adjacent slices join up with no overlap.

Dropping rows without counting them

Every filtered-out row is a decision. Count them and say how many, or you have no idea whether you removed three or three hundred.

title: 3. Collections
text:
3.8 Check yourself
Answers are at the foot of the page.



What does [10, 20, 30, 40][1:3] give?

[10, 20] b. [20, 30] c. [20, 30, 40] d. [10, 20, 30]





a = [1, 2]; b = a; b.append(3). What is a, and why?




Why can a tuple be a dictionary key when a list cannot?




You need to know whether each of a million ids has been seen before. List or set, and why?




print(some_set) gives a different order on a colleague’s machine. Is that a bug?









TipShow the answers






(b) [20, 30]. Start at index 1, stop before index 3.
[1, 2, 3]. b is another label on the same list, and .append changes the list itself rather than making a new one.
Because a dictionary key must not change after it is stored — the dictionary files it by its contents. A tuple cannot change, so it is safe; a list can, which would leave the entry unfindable. (Python enforces this: using a list as a key raises TypeError: unhashable type.)
A set. in on a set does not depend on how many items it holds; on a list it scans, so a million ids means up to a million comparisons each time.
No. Sets have no order to be wrong about. If order matters to you, that is a signal you should be sorting, or should not be using a set.





Where this shows up next
P4 iterates over these containers and makes decisions about what it finds. P8 replaces the dictionary-of-lists in the worked example with a labelled table that does the grouping for you. The counted-and-reported skipping in that example becomes the exclusions audit in P9.

text:
index and slice a list, and iterate the idea of “many values” — P3;
compare values and know what type each is — P2.








TipShow the answer





3, and the last index is 2. Length counts items; indices start at zero, so the last index is always len(...) - 1. Off-by-one errors live in that gap.
crumbs: 8  4. Making decisions, repeating work

title: 4. Making decisions, repeating work
text:
4.2 The idea
A condition is an expression that evaluates to True or False, and it decides which block of code runs:

score = 68.4

if score >= 70:
    print("distinction")
elif score >= 50:
    print("pass")
else:
    print("below the pass mark")

pass


Two things to notice, because both are Python-specific.
Indentation is syntax. The four spaces are not decoration — they are how Python knows which lines belong to which branch. Get them wrong and the meaning changes, or the file will not parse at all.
elif chains are checked in order, and stop at the first match. A score of 75 satisfies both >= 70 and >= 50, but only the first branch runs. That is why the tests must be written from most to least demanding; reverse them and everything above 50 becomes a pass.

Comparison and logic

n = 57
print(n > 50, n == 57, n != 57, 50 <= n <= 100)
print(n > 50 and n < 60)
print(n < 50 or n > 100)
print(not n > 50)

True True False True
True
False
False


== compares, = assigns. Confusing them is a syntax error in a condition, which is fortunate — in some languages it silently assigns instead.
50 <= n <= 100 chains, and reads exactly as it looks. That is unusual among programming languages and worth using.
crumbs: 8  4. Making decisions, repeating work

title: 4. Making decisions, repeating work
text:
4.3 The mechanics

for — repeat once per item

scores = [68.4, 55.1, 72.0]

for score in scores:
    print(score, "→", "pass" if score >= 50 else "fail")

68.4 → pass
55.1 → pass
72.0 → pass


The name score is created fresh on each pass, taking each value in turn. You do not manage an index and you cannot run off the end.
Three helpers you will use constantly:

groups = ["Computing", "Life sciences", "Engineering"]
counts = [69, 57, 36]

for position, name in enumerate(groups, start=1):
    print(position, name)

print()
for name, count in zip(groups, counts):
    print(f"{name:<16} {count}")

1 Computing
2 Life sciences
3 Engineering

Computing        69
Life sciences    57
Engineering      36


enumerate gives you the position alongside the item. zip walks two sequences together — and stops at the shorter one, silently, which is worth remembering.


while — repeat until a condition changes

remaining = 100.0
halvings = 0

while remaining > 1.0:
    remaining = remaining / 2
    halvings += 1

print(f"{halvings} halvings to get below 1.0, ending at {remaining:.4f}")

7 halvings to get below 1.0, ending at 0.7812


Use for when you know what you are iterating over, and while when you are waiting for a condition. The danger of while is that something in the loop must change the condition — if remaining never shrank, this would run forever. Interrupt a runaway loop with Control-C.


Tracing a loop before running it
This is the habit that matters. Take a loop and write down what each name holds after each pass:








Figure 8.1: Tracing for value in [3, 1, 4] accumulating a running total. Writing the state after each pass turns a loop from something you hope works into something you have checked.






total = 0
for value in [3, 1, 4]:
    total = total + value
print(total)

8


Three lines of paper, and you knew the answer before the machine did. Do this whenever a loop surprises you.


Comprehensions
A very common loop shape — build a new list by transforming or filtering an old one — has a shorthand:

scores = [68.4, 42.0, 72.0, 55.1, 38.5]

passed = [s for s in scores if s >= 50]
rounded = [round(s) for s in scores]

print(passed)
print(rounded)

[68.4, 72.0, 55.1]
[68, 42, 72, 55, 38]


Read [s for s in scores if s >= 50] as “s, for each s in scores, where s is at least 50”. It does exactly what the equivalent loop does:

passed_long = []
for s in scores:
    if s >= 50:
        passed_long.append(s)

print(passed_long == passed)

True


Use a comprehension when it fits on one line and reads as a sentence. When it needs two conditions and a nested loop, write the loop — a comprehension that has to be decoded is worse than the four lines it replaced.


break and continue

for value in ["68.4", "", "72.1", "stop", "55.0"]:
    if value == "":
        continue          # skip this one, carry on
    if value == "stop":
        break             # leave the loop entirely
    print(float(value))

68.4
72.1

title: 4. Making decisions, repeating work
text:
4.4 Worked example
Classifying the cohort, and counting what you could not classify.

import csv
from pathlib import Path

rows = list(csv.DictReader(Path("data/cohort.csv").open()))

bands = {"distinction": 0, "merit": 0, "pass": 0, "below": 0}
unusable = []

for row in rows:
    raw = row["final_score"]
    if raw == "":
        unusable.append((row["student_id"], "no score recorded"))
        continue

    score = float(raw)
    if not 0 <= score <= 100:
        unusable.append((row["student_id"], f"impossible score {score}"))
        continue

    if score >= 70:
        bands["distinction"] += 1
    elif score >= 60:
        bands["merit"] += 1
    elif score >= 50:
        bands["pass"] += 1
    else:
        bands["below"] += 1

for name, count in bands.items():
    print(f"  {name:<12} {count:>3}")
print(f"\n  classified {sum(bands.values())} of {len(rows)}")
for student, reason in unusable:
    print(f"  excluded {student}: {reason}")

  distinction   69
  merit        103
  pass          60
  below          6

  classified 238 of 240
  excluded S0018: no score recorded
  excluded S0189: impossible score 187.0


Three things in that loop are deliberate and worth copying.
The continue cases come first, before any arithmetic. A value you cannot use should leave the loop body before it can contaminate anything.
Every exclusion is recorded with a reason, not just counted. “Two rows dropped” invites the question “which, and why?”; this answers it in advance.
And the bands are checked from highest to lowest, because elif stops at the first match. Written the other way round, every score above 50 would land in pass and the top two bands would always be zero.

title: 4. Making decisions, repeating work
text:
4.5 Try it yourself

Exercise 1 Trace this on paper before running it. What does it print?
total = 0
for i in range(1, 5):
    total += i
    print(i, total)






TipShow the solution





1 1
2 3
3 6
4 10
range(1, 5) gives 1, 2, 3, 4 — it starts at 1 and stops before 5, the same exclusive-end convention as slicing. total += i is shorthand for total = total + i.





Exercise 2 This is meant to report every score band. Why does it always print pass for anything above 50?
if score >= 50:
    print("pass")
elif score >= 60:
    print("merit")
elif score >= 70:
    print("distinction")






TipShow the solution





An elif chain stops at the first true condition. A score of 85 satisfies >= 50, so it prints pass and the later branches are never reached.
The fix is to order the tests from most to least demanding — >= 70, then >= 60, then >= 50 — so the first one that matches is the right one.
A useful check: if any branch of an elif chain can never run, the ordering is wrong.





Exercise 3 Rewrite as a comprehension, then say whether you would keep it.
long_names = []
for name in groups:
    if len(name) > 10:
        long_names.append(name.upper())






TipShow the solution





long_names = [name.upper() for name in groups if len(name) > 10]
Whether to keep it is a judgement, and the honest answer here is yes: it fits on one line and reads as a sentence — “name uppercased, for each name in groups, where the name is longer than ten characters”.
If it needed a second condition and a nested loop, the four-line version would be clearer. Brevity is not the goal; being read correctly on the first pass is.

title: 4. Making decisions, repeating work
text:
4.6 Check it in Python
Two checks that catch the two commonest loop bugs.
Did every item get accounted for? A loop that filters should conserve the total:

values = [68.4, 42.0, 72.0, 55.1, 38.5]
kept = [v for v in values if v >= 50]
dropped = [v for v in values if v < 50]

assert len(kept) + len(dropped) == len(values)
print(f"kept {len(kept)}, dropped {len(dropped)}, of {len(values)}")

kept 3, dropped 2, of 5


If a value could satisfy both conditions or neither, this assertion fires — a > 50 written where >= 50 was meant loses every score of exactly 50, and the count catches it. What it cannot catch is Exercise 2’s misordered elif chain: that still puts every score in exactly one branch, just the wrong one. For that you need a case whose answer you already know — check that 85 comes out as distinction.
Does the while condition actually change? Add a guard while developing:

remaining, steps = 100.0, 0

while remaining > 1.0:
    remaining /= 2
    steps += 1
    assert steps < 1000, "loop is not converging — check the update"

print(f"finished in {steps} steps at {remaining:.4f}")

finished in 7 steps at 0.7812


The assertion costs nothing and turns an infinite loop into an immediate, readable failure. Remove it once the logic is settled, or leave it in — a bound you can justify is documentation.

title: 4. Making decisions, repeating work
text:
4.7 Common wrong turns

Where this usually goes wrong

Ordering an elif chain from least to most demanding

The first true branch wins, so >= 50 placed first captures everything. If a branch can never run, the order is wrong.

Forgetting that range(a, b) excludes b

range(1, 5) gives four numbers, not five. It is the same convention as slicing, and it makes adjacent ranges join up cleanly.

Writing a while whose condition never changes

Something in the body must move the loop towards ending. If nothing does, it runs forever. Control-C interrupts it.

Modifying a list while looping over it

Removing items shifts everything after them, so the loop skips values. Build a new list instead — which is what a comprehension does.

Assuming zip complains about unequal lengths

It stops at the shorter sequence without a word. If the two should match, assert that they do.

Reaching for a comprehension because it is shorter

A comprehension you have to decode is worse than the loop it replaced. Use one when it reads as a sentence.

title: 4. Making decisions, repeating work
text:
4.8 Check yourself
Answers are at the foot of the page.



How many numbers does range(2, 8) produce?

5 b. 6 c. 7 d. 8





What is the difference between continue and break?




zip([1, 2, 3], ["a", "b"]) — how many pairs, and what happened to the 3?




Why must something inside a while body change the condition?




A classification loop reports zero in your top band every time, though you can see qualifying values in the data. What would you check first?









TipShow the answers






(b) 6 — 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7. It starts at 2 and stops before 8.
continue abandons the current pass and moves to the next item; break leaves the loop entirely and carries on with the code after it.
Two pairs. zip stops at the shorter sequence, so the 3 is silently dropped. If that would be a bug, assert the lengths match first.
Because the condition is re-tested before every pass. If nothing in the body moves it towards False, the test never changes and the loop never ends.
The order of the elif chain. If a less demanding test sits above a more demanding one, the top band is unreachable — every qualifying value is caught by the earlier branch.





Where this shows up next
P5 wraps a loop in a name, so the same logic can be used in several places and tested once. P7 replaces many of these loops with a single array expression — clearer and faster, once the shapes are right. P9 does this unit’s worked example in three lines, with the exclusions written to a file.

text:
